title: Judges 1:27–36
context: The chapter now turns from particular successes to a list of what was left undone. Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth Shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, and Megiddo, and their towns; the Canaanites would dwell in that land. When Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor and did not utterly drive them out. The same refrain runs through Ephraim at Gezer, Zebulun at Kitron and Nahalol, Asher along the coast from Acco and Sidon through a string of towns, and Naphtali at Beth Shemesh and Beth Anath. In Asher’s case the wording sharpens: the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. The Amorites even forced Dan back into the hill country and would not let them come down to the valley; they would dwell in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim, though the hand of Joseph later prevailed to subject them to forced labor. The unit closes with a border notice for the Amorites. Both traditions read this list as a record of partial obedience, not as a neutral map. The repeated notice that a tribe did not drive the inhabitants out, and the choice of forced labor once Israel had grown strong, are shared ground. They should not be turned into a contrast over geography or over the refrain itself.

verses.text: Manasseh didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Beth Shean and its towns, nor Taanach and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and its towns; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Manasseh “didn’t drive out” the inhabitants of Beth Shean and its towns, nor Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, and Megiddo, and their towns; the Canaanites would dwell in that land. A string of important towns is named as left in place.

Arminian readers hear a real, responsible failure. These places were left, and the Canaanites would dwell there; the refrain is an indictment, not a mere boundary note.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the list as what Manasseh did not do. The Canaanites “would dwell in that land”: the narrator marks an ongoing presence where driving out was required.

Both traditions refuse to turn the geography of these towns into a party dispute. The shared reading is incomplete obedience, named town by town.

verses.text: When Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, and didn’t utterly drive them out.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, and “didn’t utterly drive them out.” Strength was used to extract labor, not to finish the work.

Arminian readers hear a choice made in a time of strength. They could have completed the driving out; they settled for subjugation instead. The failure is willful, not only a matter of weakness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same turn: once strong, Israel chose forced labor and did not utterly drive the Canaanites out. Chapter 2 will also speak of God’s leaving the nations; this verse first names Israel’s own compromise.

Both traditions take the forced labor as a substitute for obedience, shared ground at the heart of the list, not a contrast between the two readings.

verses.text: Ephraim didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, but the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ephraim “didn’t drive out” the Canaanites who lived in Gezer; the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them. The refrain now falls on Joseph’s other house, and the remaining people live in the midst of the tribe.

Arminian readers hear the same unfinished work in another lot. Gezer is left, and the Canaanites live among Ephraim, a settled coexistence where driving out was called for.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the notice as failure at a named city, with the Canaanites living among them, not merely nearby. The pattern of verse 28 is already at work here.

Both traditions read Ephraim’s line as part of the same indictment, without a contrast over the place itself.

verses.text: Zebulun didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol; but the Canaanites lived among them, and became subject to forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zebulun “didn’t drive out” the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol; the Canaanites lived among them and became subject to forced labor. Two towns are named, and the labor compromise of verse 28 appears again.

Arminian readers hear coexistence and labor where obedience required removal. The Canaanites live among Zebulun and are made to work; that is not the same as driving them out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same pairing of failure and forced labor. Living among them and subjecting them to labor is the tribe’s arrangement, not the completion of the command.

Both traditions take Zebulun’s notice as one more instance of the refrain, shared ground rather than a geographic quarrel.

verses.text: Asher didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Acco, nor the inhabitants of Sidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob;
verses.arminianNotes:
Asher “didn’t drive out” the inhabitants of Acco, nor of Sidon, nor of Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, or Rehob. The list is long and reaches along the coast and toward Sidon; the sentence runs on into the next verse.

Arminian readers hear how wide the leaving was. Town after town is named as not driven out; the failure is not a single holdout but a whole string of places left in peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the length of the list as part of the indictment. Asher’s lot included these towns, and the narrator will not let them pass unnamed.

Both traditions read the catalogue as evidence of incomplete obedience, not as a prompt for a contrast over coastal geography.

verses.text: but the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they didn’t drive them out.
verses.arminianNotes:
The sentence is completed with a sharper wording: “the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they didn’t drive them out.” The tribe is said to live among the land’s inhabitants, not the other way around.

Arminian readers hear the reversal as a warning. When the people will not drive the nations out, they themselves become the guests in a land still held by others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same turn of phrase. The Canaanites are “the inhabitants of the land,” and Asher lives among them because the driving out was not done.

Both traditions take this wording as a deepening of the refrain, shared ground about who, in fact, occupies the land.

verses.text: Naphtali didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Beth Shemesh, nor the inhabitants of Beth Anath; but he lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless the inhabitants of Beth Shemesh and of Beth Anath became subject to forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Naphtali “didn’t drive out” the inhabitants of Beth Shemesh, nor the inhabitants of Beth Anath; he lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless those inhabitants became subject to forced labor.

Arminian readers hear the same mixture as before: living among the nations, plus labor, still short of driving them out. The “Nevertheless” grants a measure of control without canceling the failure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let the “Nevertheless” stand as a limited result. Forced labor is not treated by the narrator as a fulfillment of the command, even when it is achieved.

Both traditions read Naphtali’s line as the refrain again, with labor as a compromise, not as a point of contrast between them.

verses.text: The Amorites forced the children of Dan into the hill country, for they would not allow them to come down to the valley;
verses.arminianNotes:
The Amorites forced the children of Dan into the hill country, for they would not allow them to come down to the valley. Here the failure is still darker: Dan is pushed back, not merely left with neighbors in the midst.

Arminian readers hear a tribe confined by an enemy that would not allow them into the valley. Incomplete obedience has become actual retreat; the later story of Dan seeking land elsewhere in the book will not surprise the reader of this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the Amorites are the ones who force and forbid. Dan is kept to the hill country; the valley is closed to them. The list has moved from leftover towns to a tribe pressed backward.

Both traditions take the verse as a severe instance of the unfinished conquest, shared ground, without a dispute over the map of Dan’s lot.

verses.text: but the Amorites would dwell in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim. Yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became subject to forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Amorites would dwell in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim. Yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became subject to forced labor. Three sites remain, and Joseph’s later pressure still ends in labor, not in a full driving out.

Arminian readers hear a partial recovery that still stops short. Joseph’s hand prevails enough to impose labor; the Amorites would still dwell in those places.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same “Yet”: Joseph prevails, and the outcome is forced labor, the compromise already named for other tribes. Prevalence here is not the same as the utter driving out verse 28 said was left undone.

Both traditions read the verse as a limited success still inside the pattern of the chapter, not as a contrast between the two traditions.

verses.text: The border of the Amorites was from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward.
verses.arminianNotes:
The border of the Amorites was from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward. The list ends with a border notice, not with a report that the Amorites were gone.

Arminian readers hear a closing line that still grants the Amorites a border. The unfinished work is, as it were, drawn on the land itself. “the rock” is not identified in the verse, and it should not be fixed as if a consensus had settled the site.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the ascent of Akrabbim and the line “from the rock, and upward” as the narrator’s southern border description for the Amorites who remain. A later reader may connect the ascent with the southern boundary language of the earlier books; the verse itself simply states the border.

Both traditions read the close as a reminder that the Amorites still have a defined presence, shared ground with the refrain that precedes it.
